verdict.reason: The one factual part of the lead (version pin) is true, but the actual vulnerability mechanism claimed — "a weak fallback RNG path for salt generation when native crypto isn't available" — does not exist in this package's real source, and the only code that would use bcrypt-nodejs for password hashing is dead/commented-out code that never executes. I read the installed bcrypt-nodejs 0.0.3 source (node_modules/bcrypt-nodejs/bCrypt.js): gensalt() always calls Node's crypto.randomBytes(BCRYPT_SALT_LEN) and on failure just rethrows the exception — there is no Math.random or other weak fallback anywhere in the file (grep for 'Math.random' returns zero hits). That documented-fallback behavior belongs to the unrelated 'bcryptjs' package's browser build, not to 'bcrypt-nodejs' — the analyst appears to have conflated the two libraries. Separately, in app/data/user-dao.js the calls `bcrypt.hashSync(...)` and `bcrypt.compareSync(...)` are literally inside /* ... */ comment blocks (lines 26-30 and 62-66); the live code stores `password` in plaintext (line 25) and compares with `fromDB === fromUser` (line 61). The CPG confirms this: querying for CpgCall nodes with name/code containing 'bcrypt' returns only the `require("bcrypt-nodejs")` call (reachable_from_entry:false) and text blobs of the surrounding comment — no bcrypt.hashSync/compareSync call nodes exist in the graph at all, because they were never parsed as live calls. So the dependency is present but functionally inert for password hashing in this codebase; the described weak-RNG password-hashing risk is not substantiated by the real source or the graph, and the analyst's own confidence was already LOW.
